title: Lua Project and Final Review
subtitle: A short practical refresher followed by 20 new application questions
description: Review the ten Lua dashboard topics. Includes three capstone examples and exactly two fresh review questions from each of Lessons 1–10.

blocks.text: Welcome to the Lua final review. This lesson is intentionally shorter on new theory and longer on practical decisions. You will revisit the ten dashboard topics and answer two new application questions for each lesson, for exactly 20 questions.

Start by reading the requirement, tracing where its data comes from, and deciding what success should look like. Then test both a normal case and a boundary or failure case. A correct program should not only work once; it should behave predictably when its inputs change.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Lua. Paste this snippet into the Lua editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 1: Lua Project and Final Review
blocks.code:
local scores={72,86,91}; local total=0
for _,score in ipairs(scores) do total=total+score end
print(string.format("Average: %.1f", total/#scores))

blocks.text: The first sample illustrates a small part of the solution. Before extending it, separate the input, the transformation, and the output. That separation makes it easier to test each part and locate defects.

A final project combines several ideas instead of treating each lesson as an isolated trick. Keep the responsibilities clear, choose data structures that match the job, and validate information at the boundary where it enters the program.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Lua. Paste this snippet into the Lua editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 2: Lua Project and Final Review
blocks.code:
local correct=true; local xp=correct and 5 or 0
print("XP earned: " .. xp)

blocks.text: Now consider how this idea would behave with empty data, invalid input, and a larger set of records. If an operation can fail, design the response deliberately rather than showing a success message before the operation has actually succeeded.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 3: Lua Project and Final Review

blocks.text: Use the third example as a starting point, then explain how it relates to the course topic: Build a final Lua project, review the major concepts and demonstrate your programming skills.

Answer two questions from each dashboard lesson. These questions are newly written for this review and are not copied from the corresponding lesson quizzes. Read carefully: select the option that best satisfies the requirement, not merely an option that could work in a different situation.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to Lua: A team receives a repository with no run instructions. What should the maintainer add to make a fresh setup verifiable?
options: A setup/run guide plus a minimal test or sample command.
Only a screenshot of the editor.
A larger logo.
A statement that setup is obvious.
blocks.explanation: A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to Lua: The app works after manual edits but fails when built from source. What should be compared?
options: The wallpaper on each device.
The actual source, compiler/runtime configuration, and documented build path.
The author’s typing speed.
The names of unrelated files.
blocks.explanation: Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — Variables and Data Types: Two components disagree about a learner’s current XP. Which refactor is strongest?
options: Keep both independent values and sync them by hand.
Show both values so the user chooses.
Use one authoritative value and derive each display from it.
Store the value in a constant even though it changes.
blocks.explanation: One source of truth avoids state drift.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. One source of truth avoids state drift.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. One source of truth avoids state drift.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — Variables and Data Types: A production setting should not change after configuration. How should it be represented?
options: As an input field that always accepts edits.
As duplicated mutable global state.
As a variable reset every second.
As a constant/immutable binding after safe configuration.
blocks.explanation: Immutable configuration communicates that the value should not be reassigned.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Immutable configuration communicates that the value should not be reassigned.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Immutable configuration communicates that the value should not be reassigned.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Operators and Expressions: A discount expression is correct for simple values but fails when several operations are combined. What is the best review action?
options: Add parentheses to make the intended grouping explicit and test representative values.
Convert the result to a sentence before calculating.
Remove the tests.
Replace all operators with addition.
blocks.explanation: Explicit grouping plus tests reduces errors involving precedence and edge values.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Explicit grouping plus tests reduces errors involving precedence and edge values.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Explicit grouping plus tests reduces errors involving precedence and edge values.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Operators and Expressions: A filter should include scores equal to the cutoff. Which requirement should the comparison encode?
options: Only values greater than the cutoff.
Greater-than-or-equal to the cutoff.
Only values below the cutoff.
A string concatenation.
blocks.explanation: The boundary condition must match the explicit inclusion rule.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The boundary condition must match the explicit inclusion rule.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. The boundary condition must match the explicit inclusion rule.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 4 — Conditions and Control Flow: A branch for a premium feature is never reached. What should be investigated?
options: The footer styling.
The size of the source file.
Whether earlier conditions already catch the input.
The names of unrelated classes.
blocks.explanation: Earlier conditions can shadow a later branch if the conditions overlap or are ordered poorly.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Earlier conditions can shadow a later branch if the conditions overlap or are ordered poorly.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Earlier conditions can shadow a later branch if the conditions overlap or are ordered poorly.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 4 — Conditions and Control Flow: A value enters from a form and controls a feature. Which approach best avoids invalid states?
options: Trust that the form never changes.
Check only the button’s caption.
Remove all constraints.
Validate the value and explicitly handle rejected inputs.
blocks.explanation: External input must be checked at the point where it becomes trusted application state.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. External input must be checked at the point where it becomes trusted application state.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. External input must be checked at the point where it becomes trusted application state.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 5 — Loops and Iteration: A report skips the final record in a list. Which class of defect should be checked first?
options: An iteration boundary/off-by-one error.
A font fallback.
A URL fragment.
An unused CSS class.
blocks.explanation: Off-by-one mistakes often arise from confusing inclusive endpoints and collection length.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Off-by-one mistakes often arise from confusing inclusive endpoints and collection length.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Off-by-one mistakes often arise from confusing inclusive endpoints and collection length.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 5 — Loops and Iteration: A processing loop may wait forever for a state change. What improvement makes it safer?
options: Remove its stopping condition.
Define a termination condition, timeout or cancellation strategy where appropriate.
Increase the loop speed only.
Hide its output.
blocks.explanation: Long-running loops need a deliberate termination or cancellation plan.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Long-running loops need a deliberate termination or cancellation plan.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Long-running loops need a deliberate termination or cancellation plan.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 6 — Tables and Data Structures: A collection is used to retrieve a learner by a unique identifier. What design question matters most?
options: Whether a map/dictionary keyed by the identifier fits the lookup requirement and uniqueness rule.
Whether the item names are colorful.
Whether the code has a heading.
Whether every collection uses indexes.
blocks.explanation: Data structures should fit the expected access pattern and identity constraints.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Data structures should fit the expected access pattern and identity constraints.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Data structures should fit the expected access pattern and identity constraints.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 6 — Tables and Data Structures: A filtered list is unexpectedly missing items after an update. What should you check?
options: Only the page title.
Whether the loop/indexing or collection mutation changes the original values during iteration.
The operating system wallpaper.
Whether comments are uppercase.
blocks.explanation: Collection mutation and index behavior can cause skipped, duplicated, or missing results.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Collection mutation and index behavior can cause skipped, duplicated, or missing results.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Collection mutation and index behavior can cause skipped, duplicated, or missing results.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 7 — Functions and Scope: Two features calculate eligibility differently after one rule changes. What is a better design?
options: Keep both implementations independent.
Put the rule in a comment only.
Share one tested function that owns the eligibility rule.
Let each screen guess.
blocks.explanation: Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 7 — Functions and Scope: A calculation’s output is needed by three later operations. Which interface is most useful?
options: Only print a decorative message.
Return nothing and rely on visible output.
Store the result in an unrelated global.
Return a value with a clear contract.
blocks.explanation: Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 8 — Modules, Metatables and OOP: A service call fails, but the application still shows “Saved successfully.” What needs correction?

Remove the error path.
Only show success after confirmation and provide meaningful failure handling.
Repeat the same request indefinitely.

Remove error handling to reduce lines.
